autor: Gregory of Tours, Histories (575–594); the Lives of Anianus of Orléans, Lupus of Troyes and Genovefa of Paris; Sidonius Apollinaris, letters (about 470–478); Bruno Krusch's verdicts (1896)
quelle: Gregory of Tours, Historiae II.5–7, ed. W. Arndt, MGH SRM I.1 (Hanover 1884), pp. 66–69 (archive.org monumentagerman01hann), English by O. M. Dalton, The History of the Franks (Oxford 1927), vol. II pp. 44–47 (archive.org historyoffranksb0002omda); Vitae Aniani, Lupi and Genovefae, ed. B. Krusch, MGH SRM III (Hanover 1896), pp. 105, 114–122, 208, 219–220 (archive.org monumentagerman03hann); Sidonius, Epistulae VII.12 and VIII.15, ed. Chr. Luetjohann, MGH Auct. ant. VIII (Berlin 1887), pp. 118, 147 (archive.org bub_gb_W-0JAAAAIAAJ), English by O. M. Dalton, The Letters of Sidonius (Oxford 1915), vol. II pp. 125, 172–173 (archive.org lettersofsidoniu02sido). All public domain.
hinweis: The Latin follows the printed editions, checked against the page images: Gregory in Arndt's text of 1884, the Lives as Krusch printed them from their oldest manuscripts, with their rustic spelling. Gregory and Sidonius are given in Dalton's English (public domain), which numbers Gregory's chapters one lower than Arndt; the Lives and Krusch's Latin verdicts are in the site's working translation, close to the Latin and dedicated to the public domain.

sections.blurb: Gregory of Tours, writing about 575–594, opens the war with a bishop who is told in Rome that the Huns cannot be stopped, and with the burning of Metz on Easter eve. He marks what he has only heard.

units.pg: Hist. II.5 · MGH SRM I p. 66–67
units.orig: Igitur rumor erat, Chunos in Galliis velle prorumpere. Erat autem tunc temporis apud Tungrus oppidum Aravatius eximiae sanctitatis episcopus, qui vigiliis ac ieiuniis vacans, crebro lacrimarum imbre perfusus, Dei misericordiam praecabatur, ne umquam gentem hanc incredulam sibique semper indignam in Galliis venire permitterit. Sed sentiens per spiritum, pro delictis populi sibi hoc non fuisse concessum, consilium habuit expetendi urbem Romanam, scilicet ut, adiunctam sibi apostolicae virtutis patrocinia, quae humiliter ad Dei misericordiam flagitabat, mereretur facilius obtinere. Accedens ergo ad beati apostoli tumolum, depraecabatur auxilium bonitate eius, in multa abstinentia, maxime inaedia se consumens, ita ut bidui triduique sine ullo cibo putuque maneret, nec esset intervallum aliquod, in quo ab oratione cessaret. Cumque ibidem per multorum dierum spatia in tali adflectione moraretur, fertur hoc a beato apostolo accepisse responsum: 'Quid me, vir sanctissime, inquietas? Ecce enim apud Domini deliberationem prursus sanccitum est, Chunos in Gallias advenire, easque maxima tempestate debere depopulari. Nunc igitur sume consilium, accelera velociter, ordena domum tuam, sepulturam conpone, require lentiamina munda! Ecce enim migraveris a corpore, nec videbunt oculi tui mala, quae facturi sunt Chuni in Galliis, sicut locutus est dominus Deus noster'.
units.en: Now there was a rumour that the Huns intended to overrun Gaul. At that time there lived in the town of Tongres Aravatius, a bishop of the most excellent holiness, who devoted himself to fasting and vigil, and often, bathed with a rain of tears, besought God's mercy that He would not suffer this unbelieving race, ever unworthy of His grace, to penetrate into Gaul. But feeling in his heart that his prayer had not been granted through the sins of the people, he formed the design of visiting Rome, that he might be strengthened by the miraculous power of the apostle, and thereby better deserve to obtain that for which he made humble supplication to God. He went therefore to the apostle's tomb, and besought the aid of his loving-kindness, wearing himself out in such great abstinence and extremity of fasting, that he would remain two or three days without food or drink, nor for a moment intermit his prayers. And after he had continued for the space of many days in this mortification, he is said to have received from the blessed apostle the following reply: 'Wherefore, most holy man, dost thou harass me? The Lord hath considered, and it is decreed that the Huns shall enter Gaul, which must be laid waste as by a mighty tempest. Now therefore hearken to my counsel; haste with speed, set in order thy house, prepare thy burial, provide a pure white shroud. For behold thou shalt depart from the body, nor shall thine eyes behold the evil to be wrought in Gaul by this people, as the Lord our God hath spoken.'
units.note: English: Dalton (1927), who numbers this chapter II.4 (5). Arndt notes that Aravatius, who saw the coming of the Huns, must have lived in the mid-fifth century, and that from the ninth century he was always confused with Servatius of Maastricht, who lived a hundred years earlier; a Life of Servatius was compiled from this chapter and the next.

units.pg: Hist. II.5 · MGH SRM I p. 67
units.orig: Hoc a sancto apostolo pontifex responso suscepto, iter accelerat Galliasque velociter repetit, veniensque ad urbem Tungrorum, quae erant necessaria sepulturae secum citius laevat, valedicensque clericis ac reliquis civibus urbis, denuntiat cum fletu et lamentatione, quia non visuri essent ultra faciem illius. At ille cum heiulato magno et lacrimis prosequentes supplecabant humili praece, dicentes: 'Ne derelinquas nos, pater sanctae, ne obliviscaris nostri, pastor bonae!' Sed cum eum fletibus revocare non possint, accepta benedictione cum osculis, redierunt. Hic vero ad Treiectinsem urbem accedens, modica pulsatus febre, recessit a corpore, ablutusque a fidelibus, iuxta ipsum agerem publicum est sepultus. Cuius beatum corpus qualiter post multorum temporum spatia sit translatum, in libro Miraculorum scripsimus.
units.en: Having received this answer from the holy apostle, the bishop hastened his journey, and returned with all speed into Gaul. And coming to the city of Tongres, he quickly provided himself with all that was necessary for his burial. Then, bidding farewell to the clergy and the other citizens, he announced to them with tears and lamentations that they should see his face no more. They conducted him upon his way with weeping and loud cries, humbly entreating him, and saying: 'Forsake us not, holy father; be not forgetful of us, O good shepherd.' But when their tears availed not to bring him back, receiving his benediction and kiss of peace, they returned home. The bishop journeyed to Maestricht, and being attacked by a light fever, departed from the flesh; and the faithful washed his body, and buried him beside the public way. How after a space of many years his blessed remains were translated, I have described in my book of Miracles.
units.note: The book of Miracles is Gregory's Glory of the Confessors, c. 71. The chapter is a story of resignation: the invasion is God's sentence on the sins of the people, and the bishop is spared only the sight of it.

units.pg: Hist. II.6 · MGH SRM I pp. 67–68
units.orig: Igitur Chuni a Pannoniis egressi, ut quidam ferunt, in ipsa sanctae paschae vigilia ad Mettinsem urbem reliqua depopulando perveniunt, tradentes urbem incendium, populum in ore gladii trucidantes ipsusque sacerdotes Domini ante sacrosancta altaria perimentes. Nec remansit in ea locus inustus praeter oraturium beati Stefani primi martyres ac levitae. De quo oraturio quae a quibusdam audivi narrare non distuli.
units.en: The Huns, therefore, issuing from Pannonia, reached the town of Metz, as some say, on the vigil of the feast of Easter, devastating all the country. They gave the city to the flames, and slew the people with the edge of the sword, and did to death the priests of the Lord before the holy altars; no spot in the town remained unburned save the oratory of the blessed Stephen, protomartyr and deacon. The story of this oratory, as I heard it from certain persons, I will now relate.
units.note: 'As some say' (ut quidam ferunt): Gregory does not vouch for the date. Hydatius, the chronicler in Spanish Galicia, also says the Huns broke into Metz, and puts the battle not far from it (module 4).

units.pg: Hist. II.6 · MGH SRM I p. 68
units.orig: Aiunt enim, quia, priusquam hi hostes venerent, vidisse virum fidelem in visu quasi conferentem cum sanctis apostolis Petro ac Paulo beatum levitam Stefanum de hoc excidio ac dicentem: 'Oro, domini mi, ut non permittatis, obtentu vestro Mettensem urbem ab inimicis exuri, quia locus in ea est, in quo parvitatis meae pignera contenentur; sed potius sentiant se populi, aliquid me posse cum Domino. Quod si tantum facinus populi supercrevit, ut aliut fieri non possit, nisi civitas tradatur incendio, saltim vel hoc oraturium non cremetur'. Cui ille aiunt: 'Vade in pace, dilectissime frater, oraturium tantum tuum caribit incendium! Pro urbe vero non optinebimus, quia dominicae sanctiones super eam sententia iam processit. Invaluit enim peccatum populi, et clamor malitiae eorum ascendit coram Deo; ideo civitas haec cremabitur incendio'. Unde procul dubium est, quod horum obtentu, urbe vastata, oraturium permansit inlaesum.
units.en: They say that before the coming of this enemy, one of the faithful in a vision saw the blessed deacon Stephen conferring with the holy apostles Peter and Paul about this destruction, and heard him say: 'I beseech you, O my lords, that by your intercession ye suffer not the city of Metz to be burned to the ground by the enemy, for there is in it a place in which relics of this your humble petitioner are preserved; but rather let the people perceive that my power somewhat availeth with the Lord. But if the evil-doing of the people is waxed so great that the city must needs be given to the flames, at least suffer not this oratory to be burned.' They answered: 'Go in peace, most beloved brother, this oratory of thine shall alone be spared in the fire. For the city we shall not obtain this grace, seeing that the sentence of divine judgement is already gone forth upon it. For the sin of the people is grown great, and the sound of their wickedness is gone up before the Lord. For this cause shall this city be burned with fire.' It is therefore beyond doubt that by their intercession the oratory remained unharmed.
units.note: Paul the Deacon took the story into his history of the bishops of Metz in the 780s, as Arndt notes. The cathedral of Metz is still dedicated to Saint Stephen.

sections.blurb: Was Orléans saved before the walls fell, or after the Huns were already inside? Gregory says before; the Life of Anianus, the most detailed telling, says after; Sidonius, the nearest witness, a generation later, speaks of 'a breaking-in but no plundering', and calls Aetius 'the liberator of the Loire'. In Jordanes (module 2) the city is Sangiban's, and Aetius fortified it in time.

units.pg: Hist. II.7 · MGH SRM I pp. 68–69
units.orig: Attela vero Chunorum rex a Mittense urbe egrediens, cum multas Galliarum civitates oppraemerit, Aurilianis adgreditur eamque maximo arietum inpulsu nititur expugnare. Erat autem eo tempore beatissimus Annianus in supradicta urbe episcopus, vir eximiae prudentiae ac laudabilis sanctitatis, cuius virtutum gesta nobiscum fideliter retenentur. Cumque inclusi populi suo pontefice, quid agerent, adclamarent, ille fidus in Deo, monet omnes in oratione prosterni et cum lacrimis praesentem semper in necessitatibus Domini auxilium inplorare. Denique his ut praeciperat depraecantibus, ait sacerdus: 'Aspicite de muro civitatis, si Dei miseratio iam succurrat'. Suspicabatur enim per Dei misericordiam Aetium advenire, ad quem et Arelate abierat prius suspectus futuri. Aspicientes autem de muro, niminem viderunt. Et ille: 'Orate', inquid, 'fideliter, Dominus enim liberavit vos hodie!' Orantibus autem illis, ait: 'Aspicite iterum!'. Et cum aspexissent, niminem viderunt qui ferret auxilium. Ait eis tertio: 'Si fideliter petitis, Dominus velociter adest'. At ille cum fletu et heiulatu magno Domini misericordiam inplorabant. Exactam quoque orationem, tertio iuxta senis imperium aspicientes de muro, viderunt a longe quasi nebulam de terra consurgere. Quod renuntiantes, ait sacerdus: 'Domini auxilium est'.
units.en: But Attila, king of the Huns, going forth from Metz, subdued many cities of Gaul; and he came to Orleans, and battered it with rams, striving so to take the city. At that time the most blessed Anianus was bishop in this city, a man eminent in wisdom and renowned for holiness, the record of whose virtuous deeds are faithfully preserved among us. When the beleaguered people cried out to their bishop to know what they should do, he, trusting in God, enjoined them all to prostrate themselves in prayer, and with tears to implore the help of God, ever present in time of need. And while they prayed according to his bidding, the bishop cried: 'Look forth from the city wall, if haply the pity of God succour us.' For he deemed that by the mercy of the Lord Aëtius should come, whom before he had visited in Arles, foreseeing that which might come to pass. So they looked out from the wall, but saw no man. Then he said: 'Pray in faith; for this day shall the Lord deliver you.' And while they continued praying he said: 'Look once more.' And when they looked they saw none that might succour them. He said to them a third time: 'If ye seek Him in faith, the Lord cometh among us right soon.' Again with many tears and lamentations they besought the compassion of the Lord. But when their prayer was done, they looked forth from the wall a third time as the old man bade them, and behold they saw afar off as it might be a cloud rising from the earth. And they brought the bishop the news, and he said: 'It is the succour of the Lord.'
units.note: English: Dalton (1927), his II.5 (6). In Gregory the bishop had gone to Aetius at Arles beforehand: the miracle and the military relief are the same event seen twice. Gregory gives no date; Arndt cites 24 June (a. d. VIII Kal. Iul.) from a Life of Anianus.

units.pg: Hist. II.7 · MGH SRM I p. 69
units.orig: Interea iam trementibus ab impetu arietum muris iamque ruituris, ecce Aetius et Theodorus Gothorum rex ac Thorismodus, filius eius, cum exercitibus suis ad civitatem adcurrunt adversumque hostem eieciunt repelluntque. Itaque liberatam obtentu beati antestites civitatem, Attillanem fugant. Qui Mauriacum campum adiens, se praecingit ad bellum. Quod hi audientes, se contra eum viriliter praeparant.
units.en: And now the walls were already shaking under the shock of the rams, and on the point of falling, when behold Aëtius came; and Theodoric, king of the Goths, and Thorismond, his son, with their armies swiftly advanced upon the town, and cast forth and flung back the enemy. The city thus freed by the intercession of the blessed bishop, they put Attila to flight, who withdrew to the plain of Méry, and disposed his forces for battle. Which when they heard, they manfully made them ready against him.
units.note: 'Cast forth' (eiciunt) may mean that some Huns were already inside. Dalton translates Mauriacus campus as 'the plain of Méry'; Arndt (1884), after Longnon, preferred Moirey in the Aube, and thought Gregory had the name from the annals of Arles. Where the field was is the subject of module 4, which continues the chapter.

units.pg: V. Aniani c. 9 · MGH SRM III pp. 114–115
units.orig: Nec inter diu spatium fuit Chunorum exercitus, rabiae saevientes, erga Aurelianes. Fossata percutiunt, omnem argumentum ingenia disponunt, quemadmodum civitatem neci traderent funditus. Continuo arietibus aptant et crebrum inpulsum certatim moenia feriunt. Alii civitatem intrinsecus cum flammis tela iactabant; at vero sanctus Anianus non iaculantium tela verebatur, sed per amblatorium muri cum choris psallentium placetis canoribus Deo modulabat. Tunc quidam episcopus, qui captus a barbaris tenebatur, clamitans sancto Aniano dixit: 'Haec, quae facere te videmus, nullius nostrorum factum profuit'. Neque adhuc, quod ceperat, medio sermone fuisset elocutus, letali est plaga percussus, ita ut in locum quo stabat continuo spirasset. Interdum Chunorum exercitus, inpellentibus cuneis, saxa murorum convellebant, uti iam civitas nullam salute habere disperasset. Domibus derelictis, omnes ecclesiae congruent; at beatissimus Anianus episcopus plebem suam orationibus verbisque specialius confortabat.
units.en: Nor was it long before the army of the Huns, raging with fury, was at Orléans. They strike at the ditches and set out every device of their engineers, to put the city to death utterly. At once they fit the rams and strike the walls in rivalry with blow on blow. Others hurled missiles with fire into the city; but saint Anianus did not fear the missiles of those who threw them, and along the walkway of the wall, with choirs of singers, he made music to God with pleasing songs. Then a certain bishop, who was held captive by the barbarians, called out to saint Anianus: 'What we see you doing has helped none of us.' He had not yet finished the sentence he had begun when he was struck by a deadly blow, so that he breathed his last at once where he stood. Meanwhile the army of the Huns, pushing with its wedges, was tearing out the stones of the walls, so that the city had now given up hope of any safety. Leaving their houses, all gathered in the churches; and the most blessed bishop Anianus comforted his people above all with prayers and words.
units.note: Krusch prints the Life as its oldest manuscript has it, in a rustic Latin that its author admits to; the English smooths it. The captive bishop is not named. On the date and source of the Life, see Krusch's verdict below.

units.pg: V. Aniani c. 9 · MGH SRM III p. 115
units.orig: Tunc e civitatem cum paucis egreditur et ad tentoria crudelissimi Attilanis se ferri iussit, rogans, ut ne ovium suarum sanguis esset effusio. Tum impius Attila dixit: 'Ut te senectuti tuae aspitio, potes adhuc nostrae provintiae custus esse ovium'. Beatissimus Anianus respondit: 'Omnes cogitationes hominum in omnipotentis Dei virtute consistunt, et qui hunc ovilem mihi tradidit custodiendum, ipse mecum ovibus meis a foveis Chunorum eripere potest'. Tunc dolore animi repletus, amariter flevit. Illico reversus est civitati, commonebat populum, ne metuerent, sed confidenter Dominum deprecarent, qui eos liberaret de potestate Attilanis. Itaque beatissimus episcopus cellula seclusus, in orationem dies noctesque pervigilans incumbebat, divinam misericordiam exorans, ut a rapacibus feris, cauli suo circumeuntibus, gregem suum custodire dignaretur inlesum. Tum caelitus inspiratus in sputum sanctus Anianus, imbrem valedissimum emisit, tridui quadriduique ingentem diluvium cum ventis procatibus miscuit, ut nullus se Chunorum ulla in parte auderet movere, donec et angelum suum in placitum Deus exhiberet.
units.en: Then he went out of the city with a few companions and had himself brought to the tents of the most cruel Attila, asking that the blood of his sheep should not be shed. Then the impious Attila said: 'Looking at you in your old age, you can still be a keeper of sheep for our province.' The most blessed Anianus answered: 'All the thoughts of men rest in the power of almighty God; and he who gave me this sheepfold to keep can himself, with me, snatch my sheep from the pits of the Huns.' Then, filled with grief of mind, he wept bitterly. At once he returned to the city and urged the people not to fear, but to pray with confidence to the Lord, who would free them from the power of Attila. And so the most blessed bishop, shut in his cell, lay at prayer watching days and nights, entreating the divine mercy that it would deign to keep his flock unharmed from the ravening beasts that prowled around its fold. Then saint Anianus, inspired from heaven, spat, and sent out a most violent rain; for three and four days he mixed a huge deluge with gusting winds, so that none of the Huns dared to move anywhere, until God should show forth his angel at his pleasure.
units.note: Attila's sentence is obscure in the Latin; it may be mockery ('old as you are, you could still keep sheep for us'). 'He spat' (in sputum): a later Life explains that he spat against the barbarians and the rain came down with it, as Krusch notes. God's 'angel' is the relief army of the next chapter.

units.pg: V. Aniani c. 10 · MGH SRM III pp. 115–116
units.orig: Neque multo post, quod bonus praedixerat vatis, aut procol ex urbi adfuit Agetius patritius cum Thursomodo rege Gothorum. In qua die, portis reseratis, Chunorum proceris civitatem introissent, omnem plebem Aurelianensium cum opibus eorum exules ducendos; iam plaustra sarcinulis honerata, familia iam parracis septus, vicissem barbari sortiebantur. Nam et haec intuens sanctus Anianus, intrepidus summa stabilitate, sedula voce populum suum commonebat, ne desperantes timerent, sed sursum Deum deprecantes corda suspenderent, qui eos eriperet de ore diaboli.
units.en: Not long after, as the good seer had foretold, the patrician Aetius was not far from the city, with Thorismod, king of the Goths. On that day the gates had been opened and the chiefs of the Huns had entered the city, to lead all the people of Orléans with their wealth into exile; already the wagons were loaded with baggage, the households were already penned in enclosures, and the barbarians were casting lots for them by turns. Seeing this, saint Anianus, unafraid and with the greatest steadfastness, kept urging his people with an earnest voice not to fear and despair, but to lift up their hearts, praying to God who would snatch them from the mouth of the devil.
units.note: The Life names Thorismod but not his father Theoderic, who in Gregory and Jordanes comes to Orléans and falls in the battle. 'Not far' renders aut procol, read as haud procul.

units.pg: V. Aniani c. 10 · MGH SRM III p. 116
units.titel: The bishop appears to Aetius' man
units.orig: Scilicet sanctus Anianus uni se ex auleis Egitio patricio manifestavit, in quo locum una cum Thursomodo apud exercitum eorum merediae resederant, et dixit ad eum: 'Perge nunc et ae filio meo Agecio, quod si hodierna die civitati venire distulerit, crastina die se autumet frustra venturum'. Ad ille sollicite interrogans, quis esset, sed subito ex oculis quam cito est proditus, tam cito in sermone recessit. Haec ut vidit, amentia perturbatus, paulolum substetit. Deinde ad Agetio patricio percurrit et ex ordine enarravit illi, ut viderat: secum patritius pertractans, prorsus alium non fuisse nisi beatissimo episcopo Anianum. Tunc eum in locum, quo se videndum prodiderat, sagaci inquisitione precepit requirendum; sed quis eorum poterat caelesti miraculo repperire? Statimque satellites suos simili dignitate consulta petit, simulque ostium suum, signum datum, arma capere edicunt, et a civitatem nostram liberanda venire nullam intulit moram. Cumque Aurelianorum Ligericae portus tetigissent, multorum Chunorum dederunt interitum. Alii vero profugi se iectu pontem, quam vimine cratis contexerant, inundante Ligere, profundabant. Nec non sanctus Anianus episcopus cum caelestem munus palmam victoriae triumpharet, solita pietate indultus, se adversantibus coram interfeci non permisit, forsitan quos repentinus furor obpressit. Nam reliquam partem Chunorum iuxta omnipotentis Dei virtutem suis orationibus effugavit et ita eos dimersit, ut neque amplius nomen eorum auditus, forsitan ut nunc memoriter personet.
units.en: For saint Anianus showed himself to one of the courtiers of the patrician Aetius, in the place where they had halted at midday with Thorismod by their army, and said to him: 'Go now and tell my son Aetius that if he puts off coming to the city today, tomorrow he may reckon he will come in vain.' The man asked anxiously who he was, but as suddenly as he had appeared before his eyes, so suddenly he withdrew in mid-speech. When he saw this, shaken out of his wits, he stood still a little. Then he ran to the patrician Aetius and told him in order what he had seen; and the patrician, turning it over with himself, concluded that it had been none other than the most blessed bishop Anianus. Then he ordered him to be sought with careful search in the place where he had let himself be seen; but which of them could find a heavenly miracle? At once he called his officers of like rank to council, and at the same time, a signal given, they ordered his army to take up arms, and he made no delay in coming to free our city. And when they reached the Loire harbour of Orléans, they put many Huns to death. Others, fleeing, threw themselves on to a bridge they had woven of wicker hurdles, and as the Loire rose they were sunk. And saint Anianus the bishop, while he triumphed in the heavenly gift of the palm of victory, moved by his usual piety, did not allow those who opposed him to be killed before him, perhaps those whom sudden fury had overwhelmed. For the rest of the Huns he put to flight by his prayers, through the power of almighty God, and so scattered them that their name was heard no more, except as it now sounds in memory.
units.note: 'Our city': the author writes as a man of Orléans. 'Except as' renders forsitan, which Krusch takes to mean nisi. The sentence on sparing the enemy is obscure in the Latin. Of a battle at Mauriacus or on the Catalaunian fields, the Life says nothing.

units.pg: Sid. Ep. VIII.15.1 · MGH AA VIII p. 147
units.orig: Dum laudibus summis sanctum Annianum, maximum consummatissimumque pontificem, Lupo parem Germanoque non imparem, vis celebrari fideliumque desideras pectoribus infigi viri talis ac tanti mores merita virtutes, cui etiam illud non absque iustitia gloriae datur, quod te successore decessit, exegeras mihi, ut promitterem tibi Attilae bellum stilo me posteris intimaturum, quo videlicet Aurelianensis urbis obsidio oppugnatio, inruptio nec direptio et illa vulgata exauditi caelitus sacerdotis vaticinatio continebatur.
units.en: You wished me to celebrate the glory of the holy Annianus, the greatest and most perfect of prelates, equal to Lupus, and no unworthy rival of Germanus; you would fain see graven on the hearts of all the faithful the memory of a character so fine, so eminent, so richly endowed with so many virtues and so many merits, to which I myself should like to add this, that he made way for such a successor as yourself. You exacted a promise from me at the same time that I would hand down for the benefit of those who come after us the history of the war with Attila, with the whole tale of the siege and assault of Orleans when the city was attacked and breached, but never laid in ruins, and the bishop's celebrated prophecy was divinely answered from above.
units.note: English: Dalton (1915), vol. II pp. 172–173. To Prosper, bishop of Orléans and Anianus' successor, about 478 by Dalton's dating. The Latin has four nouns: siege, assault, breaking-in, but no plundering (obsidio oppugnatio, inruptio nec direptio). The next sentence of the letter says Sidonius began the history and gave it up; it was never written.

units.pg: Sid. Ep. VII.12.3 · MGH AA VIII p. 118
units.orig: praetermisit Gallias tibi administratas tunc, cum maxume incolumes erant. praetermisit Attilam Rheni hostem, Thorismodum Rhodani hospitem, Aetium Ligeris liberatorem sola te dispositionum salubritate tolerasse.
units.en: It has passed over your administration of the Gauls when they were still at their greatest extent. It has been silent on the efficacy of your measures against Attila the enemy on the Rhine and Thorismond the guest of the Rhone, and on your support of Aetius the Liberator of the Loire.
units.note: English: Dalton (1915), vol. II p. 125. To Tonantius Ferreolus, praetorian prefect of the Gauls in 451, the civil officer who had to feed and quarter the armies. Literally: 'that you bore with Attila the enemy of the Rhine, Thorismod the guest of the Rhône and Aetius the liberator of the Loire by the soundness of your arrangements alone'. The one contemporary of the events who gives the relief of the Loire to Aetius in so many words.

sections.titel: Troyes: Lupus taken to the Rhine
sections.blurb: Troyes had no walls. In the Life of its bishop Lupus, the saint does not turn Attila back, as nineteenth-century pictures have it: Attila takes him along as a guarantee of his own safety as far as the Rhine, and asks for his prayers.

units.pg: V. Lupi c. 5 · MGH SRM III p. 121
units.orig: Inter haec non longa post tempora, imminentibus Hunis, quorum per Gallias ubique diffusus premebat exercitus: quippe cum diversa urbium loca simulatae pacis arte temptaret, alia excidio eruenda urgeret, Tricassinam urbem patentibus campis expositam nec armis munitam nec muris cum infensaret sui agminis densitate, sollicitus piae mentis antistes, recurrens ad nota praesidia, sola ad Deum intercessione et prece deposita, supernae opis defendit auxilio, in cuius absolutione totius discriminis conpressit incendium. Ad ille feralis Attila et immitis fidem eius altiori sensu suspiciens, pro incolumitatis suae statu vel exercitus sui salute secum indicit iturum, Reni etiam fluenta visurum, ibique dimittendum pariter pollicetur. Cui de loco confestim ut revertatur offertur, reditus non negatur, iter ostenditur; nec minus pro se orandum supplicavit enixe, interprete Hunigasio.
units.en: Among these things, not long after, when the Huns were threatening, whose army, spread everywhere through Gaul, pressed hard (for it tried some cities by the art of a feigned peace and drove on others to be torn up in destruction), and when it was assailing with the mass of its column the city of Troyes, lying open in the exposed plains and defended neither by arms nor by walls, the bishop, anxious in his pious mind, ran back to his familiar defences; with intercession and prayer laid before God alone he defended the city with the help of heavenly aid, and by its deliverance from all danger put out the fire. But that savage and pitiless Attila, regarding his faith with a deeper sense, declared that for the safety of his own person and the welfare of his army the bishop should go with him and see the waters of the Rhine as well, and promised likewise that he would be released there. There at once he is offered his return from the place; the return is not refused, the road is shown; and Attila no less earnestly begged him to pray for him, Hunigasius interpreting.
units.note: The interpreter's name recalls Onegesius, Attila's leading man in Priscus' account of the court (module 1). Sidonius' letters to Lupus, who was still bishop about 479, say nothing of Attila.

units.pg: V. Lupi c. 6 · MGH SRM III pp. 121–122
units.orig: Regressus ut vidit se suorum desperatione turbatum, ad montis perfugium Latiscone experto sollertior mox credidit festinandum, ut illic transferret plebem, quam orationum suffragiis discrimini subiacentem inter excidia publica et hostilia arma defenderat; quod perfugium distans XLV milibus ab urbe. Ubi bienni temporis spatio commanens, offensus venientium raritate suorum, Matiscone se censuit transferendum.
units.en: On his return, when he saw himself troubled by the despair of his own people, he, made wiser by experience, soon thought he should hasten to the refuge of the mountain of Latisco, to move there the people whom, lying in danger amid the public ruin and the enemy's arms, he had defended with the support of his prayers; this refuge is forty-five miles from the city. Having stayed there for the space of two years, offended that so few of his own people came to him, he decided to move to Mâcon.
units.note: Latisco: Mont Lassois near Châtillon-sur-Seine. Krusch (pp. 118–119) read the bishop's absence and the estate at Mâcon as inventions to secure lands for the church of Troyes.

sections.blurb: In the Life of Genovefa, Paris is not besieged at all. The danger is panic: the citizens want to move their goods to safer cities, and a young woman who tells them to stay and pray is nearly stoned as a false prophet. She never meets Attila.

units.pg: V. Genovefae c. 12 · MGH SRM III p. 219
units.orig: Exiente sono, Attela Chunorum regem sevitia superatum Gallia provintia coepisse vastare, terrore itaque perculsi Pariseorum cives, bona ac stipendia facultatum suarum in alias tuciores civitates deferre nitebantur. Quorum matronas convocans Genuvefa, suadebat, ut ieiuniis et orationibus ac vigiliis insisterent, quatenus possint, sicut Iudith et Ster, superventura clade evadere. Consentientes ergo Genuvefe, dies aliquod in baptisterio vigilias exercentes, ieiuniis et orationibus, sicut Genuvefa suasserat, Deo vacaverunt. Viris quoque earum idem suadebat, ne bona sua a Parisius auferrent: nam illas civitates, quas esse tutiores credebant, gens irata vastaret; Parisius vero incontaminata ab inimicis, Christo protegente, salvandam, ut factum est, adserebat. Insurrexerunt in eam cives Parisiorum, dicentes, pseudoprophetam suis temporibus aparuisse, eo quod prohiberentur ab ea quasi a peritura civitatem in alias tucioris urbis bona sua transferre.
units.en: When the report went out that Attila, king of the Huns, overcome by savagery, had begun to lay waste the province of Gaul, the citizens of Paris, struck with terror, tried to carry their goods and the funds of their means away to other, safer cities. Genovefa called their wives together and urged them to persist in fasts, prayers and vigils, so that, like Judith and Esther, they might escape the disaster that was coming. Agreeing with Genovefa, they spent some days keeping vigils in the baptistery and gave themselves to God in fasts and prayers, as Genovefa had urged them. Their husbands too she urged not to take their goods away from Paris: for those cities which they believed safer, the angry people would lay waste, but Paris would be saved untouched by the enemy under Christ's protection, as indeed happened, she declared. The citizens of Paris rose against her, saying that a false prophet had appeared in their times, because she forbade them, as if from a city that was about to perish, to move their goods into other, safer cities.
units.note: Judith and Esther, the women of the Old Testament who saved their people, are the models the Life offers to the women of Paris.

units.pg: V. Genovefae c. 13 · MGH SRM III p. 220
units.orig: Tractantibus ergo civibus, ut Genovefam aut lapidibus obrutam aut vasto gurgite mersam punirent, interea adveniente ab Alceoderense urbe arcediacono, qui olim audierat, sanctum Germanum magnificum testimonium de Genovefa dedisse, invenit per loca cives conventicola facere ac de interemptione Genovefe contionari. Qui cum consilium eorum cognovisset, et dixit ad eos: 'Nolite, cives, tantum admittere facinus. Ista, de cuius vos interritu tractatis, referente sancto Germano antestite nostro, audivimus ex utero matris suae a Deo electa. Et ecce eulogias, quas illi a sancto Germano relictas exhibeo!' Conperientes ergo Parisiorum cives, Genovefa testimonium sancti Germani Dei esse fidelissima famula, ac videntes eulogias, que illi, deferente arcediacono, fuerant allate, metuentes Deum et his qui ab arcediacono dicebantur mirantes, dissipato pravo consilio, insidiandi finem fecerunt. Inpletum est in die illa dictum apostoli, quo ait: Non enim omnium est fides; fidelis autem Deus qui conservavit vos et custodiet a malo.
units.en: While the citizens were discussing whether to punish Genovefa by stoning her or by drowning her in a deep pool, there arrived meanwhile from the city of Auxerre the archdeacon who had once heard saint Germanus give a splendid testimony of Genovefa. He found the citizens gathering in groups here and there and holding meetings about putting Genovefa to death. When he learned their plan, he said to them: 'Do not, citizens, commit so great a crime. This woman, whose death you are planning, we have heard from our bishop saint Germanus to have been chosen by God from her mother's womb. And see, I bring the blessed bread (eulogiae) that saint Germanus left for her!' Learning by the testimony of saint Germanus that Genovefa was a most faithful servant of God, and seeing the blessed bread which the archdeacon had brought her, the citizens of Paris feared God and wondered at what the archdeacon said; their wicked plan was broken up, and they made an end of plotting. On that day was fulfilled the saying of the apostle: Not all have faith; but God is faithful, who has kept you and will guard you from evil.
units.note: Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, had died a few years before 451; the archdeacon brings his gift, not his presence. The quotation is 2 Thessalonians 3:2–3.

units.pg: V. Genovefae c. 14 · MGH SRM III p. 220
units.orig: Summi antestites Martinus et Annianus pro virtutum suarum admiratione valde laudati sunt, eo quod unus aput Vangionum civitatem post pridie in bello inhermis offerendus, utriusque exercitus sevitia sedata, foedus obtenuit, alter vero Aurilianorum urbem ab exercito Chunorum circumseptam, auxiliantibus Gotis, meritis orationum suarum, ne periret, promeruit. Porro Genuvefa nonne dignum est honorari, quae idem orationibus suis predictum exercitum, ne Parisius circumdaret, procul abegit?
units.en: The great bishops Martin and Anianus have been much praised in admiration of their miracles: the one because at the city of the Vangiones, where he was to be set unarmed before the battle on the next day, he calmed the savagery of both armies and obtained a treaty; the other because by the merits of his prayers, with the Goths helping, he earned that the city of Orléans, surrounded by the army of the Huns, should not perish. Is it not right, then, that Genovefa be honoured, who by her prayers drove the same army far off, so that it should not surround Paris?
units.note: Martin at Worms (the city of the Vangiones) is in Sulpicius Severus' Life of Martin, c. 4. Here the Goths, not Aetius, are Anianus' helpers. The Life of Genovefa knows Orléans as a famous story to be measured against.

sections.blurb: Bruno Krusch, who edited these Lives for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1896, judged them severely: late, dependent, partly invented. His verdicts are part of the record and belong beside the texts; they are not the last word, and the notes say where later scholarship has gone another way.

units.pg: Krusch on the Life of Anianus · MGH SRM III p. 105
units.orig: Chunis urbem obsidentibus, teste eodem episcopus in castra Attilae se contulit, 'ut ne ovium suarum esset effusio' (c. 9), hostesque, sociis advenientibus, ab urbe ita repulsi sunt, 'ut neque amplius nomen eorum auditum, forsitan ut nunc memoriter personet' (c. 10). Cladis igitur Mauriacensis ne verbo quidem mentionem fecit, ad quam re vera Chuni pervenire non potuissent, si apud Aurelianos funditus victi essent. Nequaquam dubium esse potest, quin V. Aniani pendeat ex L. H. Fr. Uterque scriptor praeter pugnam Mauriacensem etiam Theodoridum Visigothorum regem silentio transiit solumque nominavit Thursomodum, filium eius. Praeterea biographus errorem commisit non ferendum in scriptore antiquo, contendens, Aetium rem publicam egisse sub Maioriano (c. 4), qui triennio post necem patricii imperator creatus est.
units.en: While the Huns besieged the city, on the same author's witness, the bishop went to Attila's camp 'so that there should be no shedding of his sheep' (c. 9), and when the allies came the enemy were so driven from the city 'that their name was heard no more, except as it now sounds in memory' (c. 10). So he did not mention by a single word the defeat at Mauriacus, which the Huns could in truth never have reached had they been utterly beaten at Orléans. There can be no doubt at all that the Life of Anianus depends on the L. H. Fr. Both writers pass over not only the battle of Mauriacus but also Theoderic, king of the Visigoths, and name only Thorismod, his son. Moreover, the biographer committed an error not to be borne in an ancient writer, claiming that Aetius governed the state under Majorian (c. 4), who was made emperor three years after the patrician's murder.
units.note: L. H. Fr. is the Liber Historiae Francorum, a Frankish chronicle finished in 727, not Gregory's Histories. Krusch quotes its sentence in a note to c. 10: Aetius and Thorismod came, and 'the Huns with their king Attila were defeated and laid low before the city, at the prayer of saint Anianus'. So Krusch dated the Life after 727.

units.pg: Krusch on the Life of Lupus · MGH SRM III pp. 118–119
units.orig: Hanc chronologiam falsam esse iudico fictamque totam Vitam inde ab initio usque ad finem. Lupi cum Attila congressus auctores antiquiores, id quod iam Boschius dolebat, mentionem nullam fecerunt; biographus vero non solum urbis Trecensis, sed etiam Chunorum salutem sancto attribuit, ideoque enarravit, post urbem liberatam eum ab Attila ad Rhenum tractum esse, eo quod fidem eius 'altiori sensu suspiciens' rex, se suumque exercitum cum illo incolumes ituros esse sperasset: cumque ad fluvium pervenissent, episcopum dimissum, eundem, ut pro se oraret, a rege enixe petitum esse, interpretante verba Hunigasio. Hunigasium illum Hunorum interpretem Attilamque semichristianum non leviter admiramur. [...] Haec omnia, ut sunt absurda, credi non possunt, Vitaque fabulis fictis adnumeranda est.
units.en: I judge this chronology false, and the whole Life invented from beginning to end. The older writers made no mention of Lupus' meeting with Attila, as Boschius already regretted; but the biographer ascribed to the saint the safety not only of the city of Troyes but even of the Huns, and therefore told how, after the city was freed, he was taken by Attila to the Rhine, because the king, 'regarding his faith with a deeper sense', hoped that he and his army would go safe with him; and when they reached the river the bishop was released, and the king earnestly asked him to pray for him, Hunigasius interpreting the words. That Hunigasius, interpreter of the Huns, and a half-Christian Attila astonish us not a little. [...] All this, absurd as it is, cannot be believed, and the Life must be counted among invented fables.
units.note: Boschius: the Bollandist editor of the Life in the Acta Sanctorum. Krusch put its author at the end of the eighth or the beginning of the ninth century (p. 119). The bracket marks a passage left out, on Lupus' withdrawal to Mont Lassois and Mâcon and on a raid of the Alamanni.

units.pg: Krusch on the Life of Genovefa · MGH SRM III p. 208
units.titel: 'In the later part of the eighth century'
units.orig: Scriptoribus Merowingicis, Gregorio, Fredegario, auctori L. h. Fr. omnino incognita erat V. Genovefae, primusque auctor Gestorum Dagoberti ea usus est. Cum L. hist. Fr. a. 727, Gesta autem Dagoberti saec. IX. in. composita sint, eo intervallo Vita innotuit, cuius auctor et Gregorii scripta et traditionem Passionemque saec. VIII. adhibuit. Igitur eam ipsam eodem saeculo exortam esse necesse est idque posteriore parte.
units.en: The Life of Genovefa was wholly unknown to the Merovingian writers, Gregory, Fredegar and the author of the Liber Historiae Francorum, and the first to use it was the author of the Deeds of Dagobert. Since the Liber Historiae Francorum was composed in 727 and the Deeds of Dagobert at the beginning of the ninth century, the Life became known in that interval; its author used both Gregory's writings and the tradition and Passion of the eighth century. So it must have arisen in that same century, and in its later part.
units.note: Krusch linked the Life's last chapter with the synod of Gentilly in 767. The Life presents itself as written eighteen years after Genovefa's death, as the title of a French edition of 1699 puts it. Many scholars since, notably Martin Heinzelmann and Joseph-Claude Poulin (1986), have argued for an early sixth-century date; on Genovefa, Krusch's verdict is no longer the common view.
